title: First Missing Positive
description: Brute force to optimized: linear search per candidate versus a hash set versus in place index marking.

blocks.text: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, find the smallest missing positive integer, ideally in O(n) time using only O(1) extra space. The array may contain negatives, zeros, duplicates, and values far larger than the array's own length.

blocks.title: Analogy: The First Empty Numbered Locker
blocks.text: Imagine a row of numbered lockers starting from locker 1, and a pile of tickets with random numbers on them, some negative, some huge, some repeated. Placing every valid ticket into its own matching locker number reveals the first locker left empty.

blocks.caption: Find the smallest positive integer that never appears in the array

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["1 and 2 are present","3 is the smallest positive missing","0 is not positive, so it is irrelevant to the search"],["Answer","3","every positive integer smaller than 3 is already present"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["1 is present, but 2 is not","2 is the smallest positive missing","negative and out of range values like -1, 3, and 4 do not block 2 from being the answer"],["Answer","2","every positive integer smaller than 2 is already present"]]}

blocks.text: None of the values 1, 2, or 3 appear anywhere in this array, so the smallest missing positive integer is simply 1, regardless of how large the other values are.
It helps to ask exactly how large the answer could possibly be, since that bound is the key to the fastest solution.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Contains Duplicate and Two Sum already showed that a hash set or hash map turns "does this value exist" into an O(1) average lookup, which is directly usable here, build a set of every present value, then scan candidates 1, 2, 3 upward.

Observation 2: That hash set costs O(n) extra space. But with only n elements in the array, there can be at most n distinct positive integers present, so the answer can never exceed n plus 1, a much smaller bound than it might first appear.

Observation 3: Since the answer is guaranteed to live within [1, n], the array's own n slots are already exactly the right size to act as a lookup table, if every value v within that range is placed at index v minus 1.

Observation 4: Repeatedly swapping each in range value into its rightful index, then scanning once for the first index whose value does not match, correctly reveals the answer with no extra structure at all, confirmed by tracing nums equal to [3, 4, -1, 1] through to its correct answer, 2.
Recognizing that the answer is bounded by n plus 1 is what turns an O(n) extra space hash set into an in place O(1) extra space solution, by letting the array serve as its own hash structure.
Starting from 1, check each candidate positive integer in turn to see whether it exists anywhere in the array, and return the first one that does not.

items: Starting from candidate = 1, search the whole array for that candidate.
If it is not found, return it as the answer.
Otherwise move to the next candidate and repeat.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Candidates are tried in increasing order starting from 1, since the answer is defined as the smallest missing positive integer.
Each candidate triggers a full linear search through the array, since no information from a previous candidate's search is reused.
The loop is guaranteed to terminate, since there are only n values in the array, so at most n plus 1 candidates ever need to be checked.

blocks.text: Since the answer is guaranteed to be at most n plus 1 (there are only n values in the array, so at most n distinct positive integers starting from 1 can be present), this eventually finds the correct candidate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) in the worst case, a full linear search for up to n plus 1 candidates.
Space: O(1), no extra data structure is used.
Limitation: the array is rescanned from scratch for every single candidate, when a single pass could record everything that is actually present.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: every candidate triggers its own full rescan of the array, even though a single pass could record every present value just once.

What a hash set fixes directly: recording every present value in one pass turns each candidate check into an O(1) average membership test instead of a full rescan.

Can the hash set itself be avoided: yes, because the answer is bounded by n plus 1, meaning only values in [1, n] can ever matter, and the array already has exactly n slots available.

The core idea: place every in range value v at index v minus 1 within the array itself, using it as its own hash structure, then scan once for the first index that does not hold its expected value.

Record every present value in a hash set with a single pass. Then check candidates 1, 2, 3, and so on against that set, which gives constant time average membership checks instead of a full rescan for each one.
Build a set of every present value, then scan upward from 1 for the first missing one.

blocks.caption: Optimized: record present values in a set, then scan upward from 1

blocks.text: This works because once every present value is recorded in the set, checking whether a candidate is present becomes an O(1) average operation, so scanning upward from 1 correctly finds the smallest missing positive integer without ever rescanning the original array.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to build the set and at most n plus 1 checks.
Space: O(n), for the set holding every present value.
10. Further Optimization: In Place Index Marking

The answer can only ever be somewhere between 1 and n plus 1, so any value outside that range (negative, zero, or larger than n) can never be the answer and can be ignored entirely. This means the array itself, which already has exactly n slots, can be repurposed as the hash set: place every value v that falls in range [1, n] at index v minus 1, by repeatedly swapping it into position. After this placement pass, a second pass looks for the first index i where nums[i] does not equal i plus 1, and that missing value i plus 1 is the answer. If every position matches, the answer is n plus 1.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Array state"],"rows":[["Start","[3, 4, -1, 1]"],["Index 0 holds 3, swap it to index 2","[-1, 4, 3, 1]"],["Index 0 holds -1, out of range, skip","[-1, 4, 3, 1]"],["Index 1 holds 4, swap it to index 3","[-1, 1, 3, 4]"],["Index 1 holds 1, swap it to index 0","[1, -1, 3, 4]"],["Index 1 holds -1, out of range, skip","[1, -1, 3, 4]"],["Scan: index 1 should hold 2 but holds -1","answer is 2"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: place each value at its own index using the array itself

items: The inner while loop keeps swapping the value currently at index i into its own rightful index, but only while that value is in range and not already correctly placed, which prevents any infinite loop from duplicate values.
Values outside [1, n], such as -1 here, can never be correctly placed and are simply left where they are, since they can never be the answer anyway.
The final scan finds the first index i whose value does not equal i plus 1, and that value, i plus 1, is exactly the smallest missing positive integer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each value is swapped into place at most once overall, even though the inner while loop appears nested.
Space: O(1), the array itself is reused as the marking structure, no set needed.

blocks.text: This problem is the classic showcase for "index as a hash": whenever the answer is guaranteed to lie within a small known range tied to the array's own length, the array can often be rearranged in place to double as its own lookup structure.

items: Forgetting to bound the candidate range to [1, n], and trying to place values like 0, negatives, or numbers far larger than n, which would go out of bounds.
Swapping without the equality check (nums[nums[i] minus 1] not already equal to nums[i]), which can cause an infinite loop when a value is duplicated.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["An array with no positive numbers at all","The answer is always 1."],["An array that already contains exactly 1 through n in some order","The answer is n plus 1."],["Duplicate values","The equality check in the placement loop handles them safely without looping forever."]]}

blocks.text: State the key bounding insight early: with n elements, the answer can never exceed n plus 1, which is exactly what justifies reusing the array itself as a hash structure of size n.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this without extra space", think: index as a hash, place each in range value at index v minus 1 within the array itself.
If the interviewer says "why is the answer bounded by n plus 1", think: there are only n values in the array, so at most n distinct positive integers starting from 1 can be present.
If the interviewer says "what about duplicate values", think: the equality check before swapping prevents an infinite loop when a value is duplicated.

items: Why is the answer always guaranteed to be at most n plus 1?
Why does the equality check in the while condition prevent an infinite loop on duplicate values?
How would you adapt this approach to find the smallest missing non negative integer instead?
How would you find the second smallest missing positive integer using a similar idea?
Why is the overall time complexity still O(n) despite the nested while loop inside the for loop?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space. Further optimized (in place index marking): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: hash set membership, further reduced to the "index as hash" trick, placing each in range value at its own index within the array itself.

Core Idea: the answer is always bounded by n plus 1, so only values within [1, n] matter, and the array's own n slots are exactly enough to serve as a lookup structure by placing each value at index v minus 1.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for both optimized versions.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for the hash set version, O(1) for the in place index marking version.
Most Important Observation: proving a tight bound on the answer (here, at most n plus 1) is often what unlocks reusing existing storage instead of allocating new space.
Interview Difficulty: the hash set version is easy to derive; correctly implementing and reasoning about the in place swapping, especially the equality guard, is what shows real depth.
One line memory trick: place every value at its own index, then find the first index that breaks the pattern.
